name: Front Headlock Defense
keyCorrections: If you feel the choke tightening despite chin tuck: your chin is not low enough — actively press it into your chest
If they switch to a d'arce or anaconda: frame on their head with your free arm and drive your shoulder into their chest before they can lock the figure-four
If they drop to guard with the guillotine: keep your posture tall, post a hand on their hip, and drive your trapped shoulder into their thigh
description: Protect neck, posture, and hip angle when caught in a snapdown or guillotine threat. The front headlock is the most common defensive position from failed takedowns, sprawls, and scramble exchanges.
shortInstruction: Chin to chest, control the choking wrist with both hands, keep knees under hips, and circle to the non-choking side to escape.
summary: Front headlock defense is a systematic response to one of the most dangerous positions in no-gi grappling. The priority is neck protection first, then wrist control, then base recovery, and finally escape. The system rewards timing and calm decision-making over explosive movement.
whyItWorks: Tucking the chin closes the carotid artery access and prevents the guillotine or anaconda from sinking deep
Controlling the choking wrist with both hands buys critical seconds and prevents the finishing grip from being locked
Keeping your knees under your hips creates a stable base that prevents the opponent from driving you to the mat or taking your back
Circling to the non-choking side attacks the weakest part of the front headlock — the arm that does not have the grip
The front headlock position is inherently unstable — the opponent must choose between the choke and the takedown, creating a dilemma you can exploit
commonMistakes: Looking up or extending the neck as the choke is set — this opens the carotid arteries and deepens the guillotine
Trying to bench press the opponent away — this extends your posture and makes the choke tighter
Circling into the choking arm instead of away from it — this gives them your neck on a silver platter
Staying flat on your stomach — this removes all escape routes and gives them full leverage
Waiting too long to address the grip — the longer the guillotine is set, the deeper it sinks
coachingCues: Two hands on the wrist, not the arm
Knees under hips before you move
Circle away from the choking hand

oneMinuteMode.goal: Survive and escape the front headlock position safely.
steps: Freeze and tuck your chin to your chest immediately.
Both hands grip the choking wrist — do not let them lock the finish.
Bring your knees underneath your hips to establish a tripod base.
Circle your head to the side opposite their choking arm.
Peel the choking arm across your body and recover to neutral or top position.

safetySummary: The guillotine can cause unconsciousness in seconds — if the choke is deep, tap and reset rather than risking brain injury
Some front headlock variations attack the trachea instead of the carotid — this is more dangerous and requires immediate tapping
Do not try to 'tough out' a guillotine — the damage to the neck and throat can linger for weeks
Neck cranks disguised as chokes require immediate tapping to protect the cervical spine
Train front headlock defense with progressive resistance, not live intensity

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Front headlock defense follows a strict hierarchy: (1) protect neck → (2) control grip → (3) establish base → (4) choose escape branch

decisionTree.action: Each layer reinforces the one before: neck protection prevents the finish, grip control buys time, base establishes mobility, and escape selection determines the outcome
the moment you feel the front headlock, do not explode. Freeze, tuck your chin, and breathe. Explosive movement deepens the choke.
both hands go to their choking wrist. If you can control the wrist, they cannot finish the choke regardless of how deep the arm is.
plant your far foot and bring your knees under your hips. Do not circle out until you have a stable base.
circle to the non-choking side. If they follow, switch direction. If they post a hand to block, drive into a single leg on that side.
If the escape succeeds, recover to a neutral standing position or top position with underhook control.

moneyDetails: The front headlock is the most common counter to takedowns and guard pulls — a reliable defense is essential for every grappler
A successful front headlock escape often leads directly to a takedown opportunity (single leg or body lock)
Mastering this defense removes the fear of shooting takedowns — the single most important offensive skill in grappling
The front headlock defense sequence is the same system used by ADCC champions — it is tested at the highest level
nextStep: After escaping the front headlock, look to establish your own front headlock, circle to the back, or enter a passing sequence.
fixItFast: If the choke is deep and your chin tuck is not helping: tap immediately and reset — the defense must happen earlier
If they keep sprawling you flat: do not stay on your stomach — turn to your side, frame on their hip, and create space
If they transition to a front headlock guillotine from a takedown: keep your chin tucked as you land, do not let your head pop up
If they have a high-wrist guillotine (deep chin strap): do not try to peel — post your hand on their hip and circle your head to the outside
